title: Drop one packet in HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
objective: Predict which responses stall after one lost packet in each HTTP version, and explain why.
summary: A guided walkthrough follows three files, A style.css, B app.js and C logo.png, through HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and drops one packet of response A in each. On HTTP/1.1, B and C wait behind A on the connection. On HTTP/2, all three stall because TCP releases bytes only in order. On HTTP/3, only A waits because each QUIC stream recovers its own loss. The walkthrough ends with ALPN and Alt-Svc, which choose the version. A stepper lets the learner replay the loss in each version.

guided.transcript:
# One lost packet in HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

A page needs three files: A style.css, B app.js and C logo.png. HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection, so B and C wait behind A. HTTP/2 interleaves all three as frames on one TCP connection, but when one TCP packet is lost, TCP holds back every byte after the gap, so all three stall. HTTP/3 gives each request its own QUIC stream, and QUIC recovers loss per stream, so only A waits. The version is chosen with ALPN during the TLS handshake: the client offers names, the server picks one. A server advertises h3 with Alt-Svc, and clients fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked.

**00:00 Three versions, one lost packet.** Three HTTP versions carry the same three files. Watch what one lost packet does in each version.

**00:07 Same meaning, new framing.** Methods, status codes and headers mean the same in every version. Only the framing and the transport change.

**00:15 HTTP/1.1: one request at a time.** On one HTTP/1.1 connection, the browser sends GET A, waits for response A, and only then sends GET B.

**00:24 Head-of-line blocking in HTTP.** If response A is slow, B and C wait behind it. So browsers open several TCP connections per host instead.

**00:33 HTTP/2: many streams, one TCP connection.** HTTP/2 splits messages into binary frames. Frames of streams A, B and C interleave on one TCP connection.

**00:42 One lost TCP packet stalls every stream.** A TCP packet with a frame of A is lost. TCP delivers bytes only in order, so frames of B and C wait too.

**00:51 HTTP/3: one QUIC stream per request.** HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP. Each request gets its own QUIC stream: A on stream 0, B on 4, C on 8.

**01:00 The same loss stalls only A.** On HTTP/3 over QUIC, the same lost packet delays only stream 0, response A. On HTTP/2 over TCP, all three waited.

**01:10 ALPN picks the version.** During the TLS handshake, the client offers protocol names with ALPN, such as h2 and http/1.1. The server picks one.

**01:19 Finding HTTP/3 with Alt-Svc.** A server advertises h3 with the Alt-Svc header. The client opens QUIC with ALPN h3, and falls back to TCP if UDP is blocked.

Sources:

- RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
- RFC 9114: HTTP/3 — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114
- MDN Web Docs: HTTP and web networking — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP
- High Performance Browser Networking — https://hpbn.co/
- nodejs/undici: HTTP/1.1 client for Node.js (fetch, cache interceptor, cookies) — https://github.com/nodejs/undici
guided.explanation: Head-of-line blocking moves down a layer with each version: HTTP/2 removes it from HTTP, and HTTP/3 removes it from the transport by using QUIC streams instead of one TCP byte stream.

HTTP/3 gives each request its own QUIC stream, and QUIC recovers loss per stream, so only A waits. The version is chosen with ALPN during the TLS handshake: the client offers names, the server picks one. A server advertises h3 with Alt-Svc, and clients fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked.

props.title: One lost packet: which responses stall? (highlighted = stalled or waiting)

frames.caption: HTTP/2: requests A, B and C travel as interleaved binary frames on one TCP connection.
One TCP packet that carries a frame of A is lost.
Frames of B and C arrived after the gap, but TCP releases bytes only in order. TCP does not know the streams are independent, so B and C stall too.
The retransmitted packet fills the gap. TCP releases the held bytes and A, B and C continue together.

http1-one-connection.title: HTTP/1.1, one connection: a packet of A is lost

frames.caption: HTTP/1.1 on one connection: GET A is sent. B and C wait in the queue, because the connection carries one request at a time.
A TCP packet of response A is lost. TCP must retransmit it, so A stalls.
B and C are still not sent. They cannot start until response A is complete: head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.
The retransmission arrives and A completes. Only now does the browser send GET B; C still waits.

http2-loss.title: HTTP/2 over TCP: a packet of A is lost

frames.caption: HTTP/2: requests A, B and C travel as interleaved binary frames on one TCP connection.
One TCP packet that carries a frame of A is lost.
Frames of B and C arrived after the gap, but TCP releases bytes only in order. TCP does not know the streams are independent, so B and C stall too.
The retransmitted packet fills the gap. TCP releases the held bytes and A, B and C continue together.

http3-loss.title: HTTP/3 over QUIC: a packet of A is lost

frames.caption: HTTP/3: A, B and C each use their own QUIC stream (0, 4 and 8) inside one QUIC connection over UDP.
One packet that carries data of stream 0, response A, is lost.
Streams 4 and 8 have no gap, so QUIC delivers B and C. Only A waits for the lost data.
QUIC retransmits the lost data of stream 0, and A completes.

inspect.label: Why HTTP/3 needs QPACK
inspect.text: HTTP/2 compresses headers with HPACK, which assumes data arrives in order. QUIC does not order data across streams, so HTTP/3 uses QPACK: table updates travel on their own one-way streams in one fixed order.

inspect.label: 0-RTT early data risk
inspect.text: QUIC can send a request in its first flight (0-RTT early data). RFC 9114 warns that this early data can be replayed by an attacker, so servers must apply anti-replay rules. A QUIC client address can also change during a connection.

checkpoints.prompt: Load HTTP/1.1 on one connection. Step until the browser finally sends GET B. How many responses waited for A?

goal.hint: Press Forward until in_flight shows B.

checkpoints.explanation: One HTTP/1.1 connection carries one request and response at a time, so B and C cannot start until A is complete. That is head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer, and it is why browsers open several connections per host.

checkpoints.prompt: On HTTP/2, one TCP packet that carries a frame of response A is lost. Which responses stall?

choices.misconception: Thinks TCP knows that HTTP/2 streams are independent

choices.text: None, because multiplexing removes all blocking
choices.misconception: Thinks HTTP/2 multiplexing also removes head-of-line blocking in TCP

checkpoints.explanation: HTTP/2 streams share one TCP byte stream. TCP releases bytes only in order, so the bytes of B and C that arrived after the gap wait until the lost packet is retransmitted.

checkpoints.prompt: The same packet of response A is lost, now on HTTP/3. Which responses stall?

choices.misconception: Thinks QUIC delivers all streams as one ordered byte stream like TCP
Thinks QUIC over UDP ignores lost data

checkpoints.explanation: Each HTTP/3 request uses its own QUIC stream, and QUIC tracks loss per stream. Streams 4 and 8 have no gap, so B and C arrive; only stream 0 waits for the retransmission.

checkpoints.prompt: Who chooses whether a TLS connection speaks HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1?

choices.text: The server picks one name from the client's ALPN list
The https:// scheme in the URL
choices.misconception: Thinks the URL scheme fixes the HTTP version

choices.text: The client always uses the newest version
choices.misconception: Thinks clients skip negotiation and assume the newest version

checkpoints.explanation: With ALPN the client offers protocol names in its TLS handshake, in an order it chooses, and the server selects one. Node's undici offers http/1.1 first by default, so a server that follows the client's order picks HTTP/1.1.

checkpoints.prompt: A company network blocks UDP. What does a browser that supports HTTP/3 do?

choices.text: It falls back to HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 over TCP

choices.misconception: Thinks HTTP/3 support removes the TCP fallback

choices.text: It sends HTTP/3 frames over TCP
choices.misconception: Thinks HTTP/3 can run on TCP

checkpoints.explanation: HTTP/3 needs QUIC, and QUIC runs on UDP. RFC 9114 says clients should fall back to a TCP-based HTTP version when QUIC cannot connect, for example because of UDP filtering.
